model.vision: A platform that produces predictably-engineered software and delivers and operates it on the customer's behalf.

objectives.statement: Predictable delivery: customers receive a duration, cost, and risk estimate before any code is written, and the delivered system arrives within the bounds of the chosen option.

Reliable design system: the platform provides an opinionated software design system that reliably produces maintainable applications — customers receive software engineered to a consistently verifiable standard regardless of who or what wrote it, a guarantee open-ended approaches to building software cannot make — making it the best and most efficient way to build complex applications.

Operations-first revenue with room to grow: the platform's initial commercial focus is a usage-based fee for operating delivered systems on the customer's behalf, while keeping the door open to charging for other value it creates — design and construction work, tokens, or consulting — as the business develops.

Customer self-sufficiency: the customer walks through the delivery process themselves but does not need engineering staff — the platform's AI agents play every technical delivery role (architect, senior developer, junior developer, tester, operator) while the customer remains the architect-of-record and requirements source.

Cost transparency at decision time: whenever the customer is asked to commit money, the projected operating cost is presented as a traceable, per-option figure, so every financial decision is informed by a forecast of what running the system will cost.

Extensibility to new categories of work: the platform can absorb new kinds of work products and new kinds of agents without re-architecting; the platform's delivery process remains stable as the infrastructure beneath it changes.
Audit and intervention: a human can take over, replay, or override any in-flight project; nothing the platform does is opaque or unrecoverable.

Programmatic extensibility: customers and their own tools and agents can drive the platform and stay in sync with its project state programmatically, with the same capabilities as a person using the app — integrating the platform into the workflows and tools they already use.
Accessible to non-coders: anyone who can think in systems can design, build, run, and host an application on the platform — no coding skill or engineering staff required.

The hard parts are handled: the platform absorbs the genuinely hard operational work — running systems in production, scaling, load and cost projection — so the customer never has to become an operations engineer.

Streamlined, opinionated delivery with configurable oversight: the delivery workflow is designed by the platform; how much human review it requires is configured per customer — from fully automatic to human approval at every chosen stage, with high-risk changes always human-reviewed.

model.mission: Carry each customer's idea through design, planning, construction, and operation as one guided, supervised workflow: the platform does the technical work through the agents it orchestrates and the tooling it generates, the customer stays in control through review, and the finished system is delivered — and, when the customer chooses, operated — on their behalf. The platform orchestrates; it does not hand-author code.

items.definition: The party that owns one or more projects and is billed by the platform for the services they use — today, hosting when the platform operates the delivered system.
The customer-side person who drives a project as architect-of-record — typically not an engineer — reviewing and approving the decisions their review policy routes to them.
A platform staff member with authority to intervene in a running project or operated system.
Any entity — an AI agent by default — that produces, reviews, or designs work products on behalf of a project.

A customer's undertaking to design, build, and optionally operate one software system, progressing through the system-design, project-design, and construction phases.
The durable record of a project's current phase, its design artifacts, and each artifact's review status.
A single work product of the delivery process belonging to a project — mission, glossary, architecture, plan, and so on — carrying a review status of awaiting, committed, rejected, or withdrawn.
A description of one business activity the customer's system must support, with its actors, trigger, and flow of steps.
A use case that captures the essence of the customer's business rather than a permutation of another; the small set the architecture must be validated against.
The computed duration, cost, and risk of one project option.
One candidate way to schedule and staff a project — such as normal, compressed, or subcritical — presented with its estimate for the customer's decision.
The software the platform built and now runs on the customer's behalf, consuming hosting capacity that the platform meters and bills.
The customer's choice of how far the platform's responsibility extends — building and delivering the system only, or also hosting and operating it.
The hosting and compute consumption an operated system accrues, metered by the platform and billed to the customer.
The customer's declared expectation of end-user load on the delivered application, used during project design to forecast operating cost.
The bounded time window over which a customer's metered usage is accumulated into a single service invoice.
The amount a customer owes the platform for one billing period's metered hosting usage, charged to their stored payment instrument.
The first project phase, in which the platform leads the Architect User from business vision to a validated, volatility-based architecture.
The second project phase, in which the platform turns the architecture into staffing-and-schedule options with estimated duration, cost, and risk.
The third project phase, in which Agents build, review, and integrate the system component by component against the chosen project option.
The ongoing phase after delivery, available by scenario choice, in which the platform hosts, scales, observes, and bills for the customer's system.
Capturing or refining a single design artifact together with the Architect User, whose review policy determines how it is approved at its review gate.
Forecasting what a system will cost to operate as a function of usage — at decision time from declared assumptions, and while running from observed load.
The decision point closing project design, where the customer chooses among the presented project options.
Assigning a discrete construction activity to an Agent and supervising it to completion or failure.
Evaluating a produced change against the project's design before it is accepted into the project.
Measuring construction progress against the plan at a regular cadence and triggering replanning when progress deviates significantly.
Placing a built system onto managed runtime capacity, or releasing that capacity when the system is withdrawn.
The platform's own decision to raise, lower, pause, or resume an operated system's capacity in response to observed demand, within the customer's chosen policy.
The autoscaling decision to hold an inactive operated system at zero capacity — and zero compute cost — while keeping it reachable for the next request.
Converting an operated system's observed consumption into billable usage attributed to its customer.
Pricing a customer's metered usage for a billing period and charging the resulting service invoice to their stored payment instrument.
Pausing, replaying, overriding, or taking over an in-flight project or operated system when it is stuck, unhealthy, or failing to pay.
The single per-project store holding everything the platform persists for that project — its state, its design artifacts, and its constructed outputs.
The system of record for a project's repository — where the project repository lives and its versions are kept; a hosted service or the customer's local machine.
The substrate that durably sequences and persists the platform's own long-running workflows — phase drives, billing cycles, and operation loops — across restarts and failures.
The external payment system through which the platform charges customers' stored instruments for its service invoices.

The customer's per-project choice of how much human approval the delivery workflow requires: fully automatic ('vibes'), human checkpoints at chosen stages ('checkpoints'), or human approval at every gate ('full'). Changes above a risk threshold always require human review, under any preset.
A point in the delivery workflow where a produced artifact or change waits for approval — by a human or automatically, per the project's review policy — before work continues.
A revision of an already-approved design artifact, driven by reviewer feedback or by changes to the artifacts it was based on; artifacts built on an amended basis are flagged for review.
The environment where a project's drafting and construction jobs execute — the customer's CI on their repository host, or their local machine — chosen per project as configuration.

items.statement: The platform must carry a customer through the production of a system without that customer assembling tools themselves.
The architect user must be able to co-author each design artifact with an automated assistant.
statedAs: The architect user must have a conversational surface for each Method artifact in which they can co-author with an automated assistant.

items.statement: The platform must enforce phase ordering and gate progression on artifact validity.
The platform must produce, for a planned project, multiple project options (normal, decompressed, compressed, subcritical), each with duration, cost, and risk.
statedAs: The platform must produce, for a planned system, multiple options (normal, decompressed, compressed, subcritical) with duration, cost, and risk.

items.statement: Cost estimation must be sensitive to which agents will perform which activities.
statedAs: Cost estimation must be sensitive to which workers will perform which activities.
The estimation engine must accept worker-model as an input parameter and emit an estimate per choice.

items.statement: Which kind of agent fulfills each delivery role (architect, senior, junior) must be allowed to vary.
statedAs: The construction hand-off model is policy: which kind of worker handles which Method role (architect / senior / junior).

items.statement: The platform must accept architect-user interaction over more than one entry channel.
statedAs: MCP is an entry-channel whose internal decomposition is a Client-layer choice, not an architectural pillar; read/write split is an internal MCP-server concern, not a system-level component.

items.statement: The platform must deploy and operate delivered systems on the customer's behalf.
statedAs: The platform must deploy and operate delivered systems on managed runtime, executing build and deploy through orchestrated workflows.

items.statement: The platform must produce, for a completed project, everything needed to deploy and operate the delivered system without manual handoff.
statedAs: The platform must produce, for a completed project, an artifact bundle deployable to managed runtime without manual handoff.

items.statement: The platform must serve heterogeneous and growing customer types without baking assumptions about customer size, internal team, or sophistication into its design.
statedAs: Customer types are heterogeneous and will grow; the platform must not bake assumptions about customer size, internal team, or sophistication into the architecture.

items.statement: The platform must bill customers under evolving commercial terms — initially a usage-based fee for hosting and operating delivered systems — absorbing pricing changes without re-architecting, and it never invoices for, or shares in, revenue the customer's application earns from its end users.
statedAs: aiarch invoices the user, usage-based, for hosting of operated systems — no flat subscription, no charge for construction or LLM work; it does not invoice for, or share in, end-user revenue.

aiarch bills the user for hosting of operated systems on a usage-based basis (no flat subscription); construction runs on the user's own Claude Code account and GitHub Actions — aiarch does not charge for construction or LLM work. aiarch is merchant of record only for its own invoices and never touches end-user revenue.

items.statement: All state and source the platform produces for a customer must reside in one customer-owned store per scenario, owned outright and retrievable by the customer at any time.
statedAs: Everything aiarch persists — project state (typed Method models as JSON) and source/charts/manifests — lives in one git target per scenario: the user's own GitHub (via a GitHub App) in the cloud scenarios; aiarch orchestrates via the GitHub API and the user owns the repo and their code outright.

items.statement: The platform orchestrates and observes construction while build, test, and deployment execute on the project's configured construction venue.
statedAs: The platform orchestrates construction; the build/test/push runs on the user's own GitHub Actions (cloud) or a local runner (LOCAL), dispatched and observed by aiarch via the ConstructionPipelineAccess seam.

items.statement: The platform must support pause, replay, override, and human takeover of any in-flight construction activity.
The platform must automatically adjust an Operated System's capacity (scale up, scale down, scale to zero, resume-to-baseline) from observed telemetry, per a customer-tunable policy.
statedAs: The platform must automatically adjust an Operated System's capacity (scale up, scale down, idle-pause, resume-to-baseline) from observed telemetry, per a customer-tunable policy; the autoscaler publishes revised desired state and never drives convergence directly.

items.statement: The platform must expose, for any Operated System, the current cost run-rate, projected monthly cost, and a what-if scale curve, so the Operator and the Customer can see how operating cost responds to load.
Project estimation at SDP-review time must include a usage-to-operating-cost curve and a sensitivity band for ± uncertainty around the customer's declared expected usage, per project option.
statedAs: Project estimation at SDP-review time must include a usage-to-operating-cost curve and a sensitivity band for ± uncertainty around the customer's declared usage assumptions, per project option.

items.statement: The platform must support an evolving, curated set of infrastructure building blocks for deployed customer systems, such that adding or retiring a building block is absorbed without re-architecting.
statedAs: Customer apps deployed by aiarch use a curated, evolving set of infrastructure constituents (launch set: Go + Temporal + Postgres + Git + S3); the supported set evolves and worker generation, autoscaling, and cost projection adapt via Strategy registrations on the affected components.

items.statement: Review gating must be configurable per project: the customer chooses which gates require human approval and which approve automatically, while changes above a risk threshold always require human review.
statedAs: Founder direction (2026-07-20): some customers run 'vibes' (fully automatic); serious customers require human approval at chosen stages; review/approval requirements are configured per customer.

items.name: System Design Phase Workflow
items.rationale: The sequence of Phase 1 activities (business alignment → requirements analysis → volatility identification → core use cases → architecture → operational concepts → standard check) will evolve as architectural taste matures: new sub-skills added (security review, accessibility review), existing ones reordered, gating rules changed, artifact schemas refined. A customer completing a project today and starting another in 18 months will encounter an evolved Phase 1 step set, and the platform must absorb that evolution without being rebuilt. Evolves independently of Phase 2.

items.name: Project Design Phase Workflow
items.rationale: The sequence of Phase 2 activities (planning assumptions → activity list → network → normal/decompressed/subcritical/compressed → risk modeling → SDP review) will evolve as project-planning sophistication grows: cone-of-uncertainty intervals replacing 5-day quanta, new option types, a new operational-risk curve. Evolves independently of Phase 1 — improvements to the SDP review do not in themselves change requirements scrubbing. Lives on axis 1 because the platform evolves it for everyone at once.

items.name: Construction Phase Workflow
items.rationale: The sequence of Phase 3 activities (hand-off model → per-component contract design → construction → weekly tracking → scope-change handling) will evolve as construction practice matures: continuous earned-value replacing weekly tracking, automatic contract-drafting at hand-off, AI-driven scope-change proposals. Evolves independently of Phase 1 and Phase 2.

items.name: Operation Phase Workflow
items.rationale: The choreography by which the platform operates a delivered system — the deploy-after-construction ceremony, reconcile cadence, the health→intervention→autoscale sequencing, delinquency application, withdraw — will evolve as operating practice matures: event-driven reconciliation replacing polled sweeps, progressive-delivery gates (canary, automatic rollback) in the deploy step, self-healing sequences before escalation. Same shape as the three Method-phase workflow volatilities: what varies is the Manager's activity sequence, NOT the policies it consults (Intervention Policy, Autoscaling Policy) nor the runtime it drives (Operated Runtime) nor where it records state (Operational State Store). Evolves independently of the delivery phases and of the billing cycle.

items.name: Billing Workflow
items.rationale: The choreography of a billing cycle — read cycle usage, compute the charge, execute the charge, record the outcome, unpaid-charge sweeps, dunning, delinquency escalation — will evolve: dunning sequences, proration on mid-cycle plan changes, pre-authorization holds before large charges. Deliberately distinct from Service Pricing (the pricing policy BillingEngine pivots on — what the charge IS) and from Merchant Gateway Provider (which gateway executes the money movement): what varies here is the cycle's activity sequence itself.

items.name: Construction Estimation Model
items.rationale: How construction duration, cost, and risk are computed will change as agents change, as historical data accumulates, and as the team refines the model. Construction estimation only — the operating-side forecast is split out as Operation Estimation Model. The two evolve on independent timelines (construction estimation matures with agent/build telemetry; operation estimation matures with fleet/usage telemetry).

items.name: Operation Estimation Model
items.rationale: How operating cost is forecasted as a function of usage. Used at design-time (SDP review: usage-to-operating-cost curve + operating-cost sensitivity forecast) and at op-time (OperationsManager: current run-rate, projected monthly cost, what-if curve over observed usage). Evolves as telemetry deepens and as Customer App Infrastructure expands. Independent of Construction Estimation Model because the inputs differ (usage curves + infrastructure cost model vs. build graph + agent throughput) and the outputs serve different decisions.

items.name: Customer App Infrastructure
items.rationale: The list of technologies that a customer's deployed app is permitted to use. Launch set: Go + Temporal + Postgres + Git + S3. The list evolves as the platform broadens (e.g., adding pgvector for AI-feature apps, WASM compute units). The fact of constraint is a design given; the contents of the constrained set is what is volatile — and it broadens for every customer at once. Encapsulated by OperatedRuntimeAccess — the runtime surface through which building blocks reach a customer app — with per-kind Strategy registrations on AutoscalerEngine and OperationEstimationEngine adapting their models as the set evolves.

items.name: Service Pricing
items.rationale: How the platform prices its own service evolves system-wide over time. Current instance: a usage-based hosting fee for operated systems (DEPLOYED — OPERATED); construction currently runs on the customer's own agentic-coding subscription and CI minutes. Tomorrow: per-seat tiers, free-tier subsidies, hosting-resource-class pricing, volume discounts, charges for design/construction work or consulting. This is open-ended, will ripple, and must not be a hardcoded constant — it is the policy billingEngine pivots on as a Strategy. Lives on axis 1 because the platform re-prices its service for everyone as its cost structure and market position change.

items.name: Intervention Policy
items.rationale: What counts as 'stuck', who is notified, when a human is paged, and what authority they have to override is policy that will change as the platform matures. Trigger surface includes construction variance, unhealthy operated state, and billing failures (a user's stored instrument declines a platform service invoice). Early on, every variance escalates to a single operator. Later, severity tiers, customer SLA classes, and self-healing rules emerge.

items.name: Review Policy
items.rationale: At the same moment, different customers run different review policies: one runs fully automatic ('vibes'), another requires human approval at every gate ('full'), a third takes human checkpoints at chosen stages. The policy spans the whole delivery workflow — design-artifact gates and construction change review — and covers both how much work is automated versus human-approved (absorbing the former Construction Hand-Off Policy) and who must review a produced change, from what perspective, against which reference artifacts. A non-overridable risk floor keeps high-risk changes human-reviewed under any preset. The rule set also matures over time, but the dominant axis is per-customer variance at one moment. Encapsulated by ReviewEngine.

items.name: Autoscaling Policy
items.rationale: At the same moment, different operated apps run different capacity policies: SLA-class tiers, per-app scale-to-zero thresholds, scale-from-zero cold-start tolerance, predictive vs. reactive scaling, operator overrides. What counts as 'this app's capacity is right' for one customer's app is wrong for another's. The rule set also matures over time, but the dominant axis is per-app/per-customer policy variance at one moment. Symmetrical with Intervention Policy in shape but structurally distinct: Intervention Policy answers 'is this app broken and what do we do?'; Autoscaling Policy answers 'is this app's capacity right and what do we do?' Two axes, two encapsulators.

items.name: Customer Interaction Channel
items.rationale: Different customers reach the platform through different entry channels at the same moment. Today: a browser hitting the JSON HTTP API, an MCP client (remote MCP over HTTP), and the scheduler's machine-initiated triggers. Tomorrow: IDE plugins, Slack apps, agentic clients, voice. The kind of caller is what varies. Encapsulated by the Client tier — each Client component (WebClient, MCPClient, SchedulerClient) owns one channel's specifics, including its own wire-level transport stack (JSON-over-HTTP today, streaming transports tomorrow), so a channel keeps its identity while its transport changes and Managers never see either.

items.name: Workflow Execution Substrate
items.rationale: Which durable-execution substrate sequences Manager workflow code. Temporal today; other durable executors later — the platform may migrate substrate over its lifetime, and the same Manager code must run unchanged. The executeWorkflow/signal/query/timer/schedule verbs are stable while the runtime behind them varies. Encapsulated by the message-bus utility (deliverSignal + registerSchedule) for cross-Manager control-plane verbs — reworded 2026-08-01 (Task 11 design amendment): durableExecutionAccess was reclassified from a ResourceAccess to this Manager-only Utility at the Task 7b reconciliation (founder ruling R-F); a Manager's own in-workflow primitives are execution substrate per the operational-concepts decision. The embedded test executor is an implementation profile, not a customer-facing axis.

items.name: Agentic Job Venue
items.rationale: Which CI/agentic-pipeline system executes dispatched agentic jobs — Phase-1/2 drafting and Phase-3 construction alike. Current instances: the customer's own GitHub Actions running their agentic-coding tooling, or their local machine's runner; instance set grows (other CI systems, other coding agents); the dry-run/test profile is a stubbed instance behind the same verbs. At one moment different customers run different job targets — it is THEIR venue — and a customer can migrate venue without any Manager change. The submit/observe/cancel verbs are stable; the execution system behind them is what varies. Encapsulated by agenticJobAccess. Split out of the former Durable Execution Runtime axis: the job target varies per customer with their venue choice, while the durable Manager-sequencing substrate varies by platform migration — two independent axes, two encapsulators.

items.name: Operated Runtime
items.rationale: Same shape as Durable Execution Runtime but for the runtime that hosts delivered systems in the DEPLOYED — OPERATED scenario. Today: GitOps over Kubernetes via Argo CD + Argo Rollouts on the platform's hosting cluster. Three faces: convergence infrastructure (how desired-state-in-the-repo becomes actual-state-in-the-cluster), compute cost attribution (per-customer cost-of-goods surface), and runtime-status transport (how the platform learns about state changes in the operated runtime). All three encapsulated behind OperatedRuntimeAccess.

items.name: Source Control Target
items.rationale: At the same moment, different scenarios put the per-project repo — and everything the platform does through it — on different source-control providers/targets. Current instances: the user's own GitHub (via a GitHub App, cloud), the customer's local machine (GitLocal), and an ephemeral throwaway git repo (test); GitLab later. The axis covers both faces of the provider, which co-vary when the provider swaps: (1) the persistence target for typed project state and Phase-3 construction outputs (stable verbs: createProject / readProject / commit / stageArtifact / storeConstructionOutput / retrieveOutputTree), and (2) the provider's collaboration/authorization surface (app installation and tokens, secrets, branch protection, branches, pull requests, reviews, merges). One axis fronted by three ResourceAccess components under the ratified facet doctrine (see operational concepts), one per stable verb family: projectStateAccess (typed state), artifactAccess (construction outputs), sourceControlAccess (collaboration/authorization). The former 'GitHubAppLifecycle' is a mechanism of the current GitHub instance, not an axis of change.

items.name: Merchant Gateway Provider
items.rationale: Which merchant gateway executes the platform's money movement — charging customers for cycle amounts and validating stored instruments. Stripe today (charge-only); the platform may change or add providers over its lifetime. The verbs are stable (chargeCustomer / validateStoredInstrument); the gateway behind them — its idempotency mechanics and webhook shapes — is what varies. Encapsulated by merchantGatewayAccess.

items.name: Operational State Store
items.rationale: Which storage substrate holds the platform's own operational records — operated-system state, billing state, usage log, and (2026-08-02) the episode ledger. Postgres for state/usage/billing, a local gitignored sidecar for episode traces today; managed alternatives and a deployed episode profile later, potentially migrating per record family over the platform's lifetime. The atomic business verbs on each record family are stable; the substrate behind them — engine, consistency mechanics, hosting — is what varies. One axis fronted by four ResourceAccess components, one per verb family: operatedSystemStateAccess, billingStateAccess, usageAccess, episodeAccess (ratified facet doctrine — see operational concepts). Deliberately distinct from Source Control Target: transactional row/append stores, not the per-project git repo.

rejected.name: Customer Interaction Transport
rejected.reason: Folded into Customer Interaction Channel (2026-07-22): wire mechanics for a fixed caller kind never ripple past the single Client component that owns the channel — each Client owns its own transport stack, so a separate system-level entry added noise. SchedulerClient re-tagged as a Channel binding.

rejected.name: Construction Hand-Off Policy
rejected.reason: Folded into Review Policy (2026-07-22): how much work is automated versus human-approved is the same per-customer policy the review presets (vibes/checkpoints/full) configure; a separate volatility and its HandOffEngine encapsulator duplicated ReviewEngine's axis. HandOffEngine retired with it.

rejected.name: Work Tracking
rejected.reason: Descoped by founder ruling (2026-07-20): the customer's external work-item tracker is not a platform concern; programmatic extensibility (objective 8 — agents over MCP, apps over the API) is the surface through which external trackers can sync. WorkItemAccess and WorkItemTracker removed with it.

waivers.justification: WAIVED (Refreshed 2026-07-22 (reconciliation)): 19 volatilities — 13 same-customer-over-time, 6 all-customers-at-one-moment — still over the 6-15 target. Down from 22: Customer Interaction Transport folded into Channel, Construction Hand-Off Policy folded into Review Policy, Work Tracking descoped; the three folds are recorded in the volatilities rejected ledger. Every remaining entry has exactly one named encapsulator (or a ratified facet group) and requirement traces. Re-evaluate if the count grows past 25.

Whatever the artifact set or drafting tooling becomes, a business that delivers predictably-engineered software must always carry the customer's idea through a supervised design; remove this and the platform is a code generator, not a delivery business.

Venues, agents, and code generation will all churn, but orchestrated construction of the customer's system is what the business does — the mission's 'the platform orchestrates; it does not hand-author code' made operational.

waivers.guideline: Golden Engines-to-Managers ratio — fewer Engines than Managers (the book's expectation).
waivers.justification: WAIVED (Refreshed 2026-07-22 (reconciliation)): 7 Engines against 5 Managers still inverts the book's ~3-for-5 ratio. HandOffEngine was retired (hand-off policy folded into Review Policy / ReviewEngine). Remaining consolidation candidates examined and rejected: EstimationEngine + OperationEstimationEngine encapsulate two independently-evolving estimation models with disjoint caller sets; InterventionEngine + AutoscalerEngine encapsulate distinct policies with different reuse profiles. Each of the 7 Engines has a 1:1 volatility-to-encapsulator relationship. design-health-engine joined the Engine set 2026-08-01 (founder ruling R-F: its call carries the ci-check business verdict in uc1's chain — an evaluation Strategy, not ambient infrastructure); its 1:1 relationship holds as a shared System Design Phase Workflow facet with the Manager (workflow choreography vs rule evaluation). Re-evaluate at the next scope-change replan.

waivers.guideline: Engine names are gerunds (ch. 3 naming rule: gerund + Engine suffix, e.g. MatchingEngine).
waivers.justification: WAIVED (Refreshed 2026-07-22 (reconciliation)): 6 of 7 Engines are noun-named rather than gerund-named (EstimationEngine, OperationEstimationEngine, InterventionEngine, AutoscalerEngine, ReviewEngine, DesignHealthEngine; only BillingEngine conforms). The rule is a readability convention, not a structural one. Renaming cascades through component ids, serviceContracts keys, and Go packages while construction is active — apply gerund names opportunistically whenever an architectural change next touches a given Engine's contract.

attestations.guideline: Never design against requirements; design against volatility.
attestations.justification: Attested 2026-07-22: decomposition follows the 19-item volatilities slot; no component is named after a feature, use case, or domain noun; every component blurb cites its volatility. Re-staged 2026-08-01 (Task 11 design amendment — call-chain realization, steps model, coverage reconciliation, align-up rail calls): unaffected.

attestations.guideline: Avoid functional decomposition — no container or component named after a feature.
attestations.justification: Attested 2026-07-22: component roster contains no feature-named containers (no *Processing, *Reporting, per-use-case services). Re-staged 2026-08-01 (Task 11 design amendment — call-chain realization, steps model, coverage reconciliation, align-up rail calls): unaffected.

attestations.guideline: Decompose based on volatility — every component cites a volatilities entry.
attestations.justification: Refreshed 2026-07-22 (reconciliation): every Manager, Engine, and ResourceAccess carries an encapsulates citation into the 19-item volatilities slot; Customer Interaction Channel is bound by the three Client components and Customer App Infrastructure is owned by OperatedRuntimeAccess (recorded in both the volatility rationale and the component blurb). Re-staged 2026-08-01 (Task 11 design amendment — call-chain realization, steps model, coverage reconciliation, align-up rail calls): unaffected.

attestations.guideline: Composable design — non-core use cases trace through existing components without modification.
attestations.justification: Attested 2026-07-22: all 11 non-core variations trace through existing components without modification — each carries its own step-keyed dynamic-view realization in the committed System (the founder's total-coverage extension), none required a new component. Smallest-set (ch. 4) extension, attested 2026-07-30: at 37 components the roster still exceeds the book's dozen-or-two guidance, but the smallest-set discipline was applied directly in the 2026-07-22 reconciliation that consolidated 43→37 (HandOffEngine cut; the four facet ResourceAccess folded into ProjectStateAccess; RevenueLedgerAccess folded into BillingStateAccess) — each cut a diminishing-returns judgment that a separate component encapsulated no distinct volatility. The residual size is consciously carried by the §2d ratio waiver, and further shrink awaits subsystem partitioning. Re-staged 2026-08-01 (Task 11 design amendment): wording updated to step-keyed realization language — all 16 dynamic views (core + variation) now carry realized step tables, none required a new component.

attestations.guideline: Features as integration, not implementation — no Manager named for a feature.
attestations.justification: Attested 2026-07-22: the 5 Managers are named for phase workflow families, not features; features arrive as integration (new step-keyed realizations), not new components. Re-staged 2026-08-01 (Task 11 design amendment): wording updated to step-keyed realization language — the coverage reconciliation's two retroactive activities (C-AA, C-DH) and the align-up rail calls are both integration onto existing components, not new ones.

Attested 2026-07-22 (Phase-1 half): design IS iterative here — the draft→critique→review→amend loop with staleness propagation is the mechanism; the build-incrementally half is Phase-3's. Re-staged 2026-08-01 (Task 11 design amendment — call-chain realization, steps model, coverage reconciliation, align-up rail calls): unaffected.

attestations.guideline: Volatility decreases top-down through the layers.

Re-staged 2026-08-01 (Task 11 design amendment — call-chain realization, steps model, coverage reconciliation, align-up rail calls): unaffected.

model.notes: Team: solo founder (bus-factor-1) + up to 3 concurrent Claude agent streams (architect/PM/product-manager/specialist roles). Founder works ~2 effective days/week (40% of nominal). Parallelism cap: 3 in-flight agent streams; beyond that, founder review quality degrades. Infrastructure: Go + Temporal + Postgres (CNPG for Temporal + billing head-state only; project state is JSON-in-git with git-ref CAS). Construction CI is the user's own GitHub Actions running claude-code-action — the platform holds no LLM key and does not charge for construction. Billing model (2026-06-09 MoR-reversal): pure one-directional vendor charge — the platform bills the user a usage-based HOSTING fee only (DEPLOYED — OPERATED scenario); no flat subscription; no revenue share; no charge for construction or LLM work; revenueShare=0 (no payout; the old merchant-of-record / revenue-share model was reversed). computeCost=2 (tieredFloors: tier floors + free-tier subsidies per ServicePricing strategy); schedule=1 (monthly billing period). Risk flags: bus-factor-1; founder availability variable (2d/wk); operated runtime unchosen; durable execution platform unchosen; git-as-project-state-store novelty; AI-agent construction quality variance; dog-food chicken-and-egg. No hard external deadlines. Internal-only v1 audience.

cases.title: Duplicate ExecuteNextActivity with the same tickID is idempotent
cases.proves: Scheduler retries must not double-dispatch: the same tickID must not open a second branch/PR or spend LLM tokens twice (RA-idempotency promoted to the client surface).
cases.expectedOutcome: The second call with the identical tickID does not produce a second dispatch of the same activity (dispatched=false, or the same activityId with no new branch/PR).

steps.assertion: First call dispatches C-BILLENG and opens exactly one branch/PR.
Same tickID replayed -> no second dispatch of C-BILLENG; the branch/PR count for the activity is unchanged.

scenarios.title: Operate a Delivered System (client ops: operateDeliveredSystem / readOperatedSystemView)
scenarios.description: Black-box exercise of the operationsManager surface. Proves deploy->reconcile->observe reaches Healthy; breaks it with the delinquency pause path, deploy idempotency on a duplicate changeId, and terminal withdrawal.

cases.title: Deploy after construction, reconcile, and observe Healthy
cases.proves: A full-bundle deploy publishes desired state and the reconcile loop drives the app to Healthy (mirrors uc4: deployAfterConstruction -> publishDesiredState -> reconcileOperatedState -> getApplicationHealth).
cases.expectedOutcome: DeployResult.published=true; ReconcileResult shows a Pending->Healthy transition; QueryOperatedSystemView reports Phase=RuntimeStatusHealthy.

steps.assertion: reason=1 (ReasonDeployAfterConstruction), patchKind=1 (PatchFullBundle); published=true with a non-null revision.
observed>=1 and transitions>=1 - a status transition (Pending->Healthy) is recorded on change only.
readOperatedSystemView surface: Phase=2 (RuntimeStatusHealthy), InFlight=false, CurrentRunRate present.

cases.title: Delinquency policy pauses (not withdraws) the operated system
cases.proves: The queued Manager->Manager delinquency signal must PAUSE the system when pauseNotWithdraw=true and must be observable - never silently withdraw or ignore it.
cases.expectedOutcome: After ApplyDelinquencyPolicy, publishDesiredState fires with reason=ReasonDelinquency and the view is NOT RuntimeStatusWithdrawn.

steps.assertion: pauseNotWithdraw=true; the manager re-publishes desired state with reason=4 (ReasonDelinquency).
Phase is paused (e.g. 1 RuntimeStatusPending / degraded), and specifically NOT 4 (RuntimeStatusWithdrawn) - pause is reversible when payment clears.

cases.title: Duplicate DeployAfterConstruction with the same changeId is idempotent
cases.proves: Deterministic manifest paths mean a replayed changeId must not create a divergent desired-state revision (RA idempotency asserted black-box at the client surface).
cases.expectedOutcome: Both calls return published=true with the SAME revision; the runtime is not published to twice.

steps.assertion: First deploy with changeId=chg-deploy-001 yields revision rev-1.
Replayed changeId returns the SAME revision (rev-1) - no second revision, no divergent desired state.

cases.title: Withdrawal is terminal; reconcile does not resurrect a withdrawn app
cases.proves: After WithdrawSystem the app must reach RuntimeStatusWithdrawn and the reconcile loop must not republish it - exposing any resurrection bug.
cases.expectedOutcome: WithdrawResult.withdrawn=true; the view Phase=RuntimeStatusWithdrawn; a scoped reconcile republishes 0.

steps.assertion: withdrawn=true; desired state is torn down.
republished=0 - a withdrawn app is not resurrected by reconcile; QueryOperatedSystemView shows Phase=4 (RuntimeStatusWithdrawn).

scenarios.title: Bill the User for Usage (client op: closeBillingCycle)
scenarios.description: Black-box exercise of the billingManager close-cycle surface (the constructed contract: CloseBillingCycle / RunShortfallSweep). Proves a cycle closes into exactly one computed signed net routed exactly once through the merchant gateway; breaks it with a duplicate close (idempotency / no double money move) and a gateway decline (shortfall sweep path, no phantom billing). Step inputs are grounded in the uc5 dynamic-view signatures (closeBillingCycle(customerId, cycleId), etc.). NOTE: billing is deferred build scope — the backing RAs (billingState, revenueLedger, merchantGateway) are generated not-implemented stubs on main; this scenario activates with that scope.

cases.title: Close a billing cycle -> compute net -> route money once
cases.proves: Closing a cycle reads revenue + usage, computes the signed net, routes it exactly once, and settles the cycle (mirrors uc5: closeBillingCycle -> readBilling -> readRange x2 -> ComputeNet -> charge|payout -> settleCycle).
cases.expectedOutcome: Exactly one settled cycle is recorded for (customer, cycle); the gateway moves money once under Idempotency-Key settle:cust-88:2026-06.

steps.assertion: One settled cycle is recorded for cust-88/2026-06; usageAccess.ReadRange, revenueLedgerAccess.ReadRange, billingEngine.ComputeNet, and exactly one merchantGatewayAccess.ChargeCustomer OR PayoutCustomer occur; no error.

cases.title: Duplicate closeBillingCycle for the same cycle does not move money twice
cases.proves: The load-bearing money-safety invariant: replaying closeBillingCycle for the same (customer, cycle) must not produce a second billing or a second gateway money move (same Stripe Idempotency-Key; settleCycle applied_mutation dedup).
cases.expectedOutcome: The second close is a no-op with respect to money: settled-cycle count stays 1 and the gateway is not invoked a second time.

steps.assertion: First close settles the cycle and moves money once.
Replay for the same cycle: still exactly one billing; the gateway is NOT re-invoked (Idempotency-Key settle:cust-88:2026-06 dedupes). No double move.

cases.title: Gateway decline leaves the cycle unsettled and drives the shortfall sweep - no phantom billing
cases.proves: A declined shortfall charge must surface as a failure and leave the cycle open (feeding DecideOnBillingFailure / the delinquency path), never record a billing that did not collect.
cases.expectedOutcome: chargeCustomer declines; the cycle is not marked settled; runShortfallSweep re-attempts the open shortfall without duplicating it.

steps.assertion: merchantGatewayAccess.ChargeCustomer returns card_declined; the cycle stays unsettled, no billing is recorded; interventionEngine.DecideOnBillingFailure chooses Retry | Escalate | Delay.
The sweep re-attempts the single open shortfall for cust-declined-99; it does not create a second billing and it feeds ApplyDelinquencyPolicy if it keeps failing.
